brief.situation: You are a licensed professional counselor. Daniel Kim, 29 (a fictional client), came to you for constant worry and was diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder at intake. You agreed on weekly supportive, person-centered counseling and a GAD-7 each session. This is session nine. His scores are in the chart. You have 50 minutes.
handover: Treatment plan (intake): 'reduce worry and improve functioning at work'; no measurable goals; review at session eight (not yet done).
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Daniel answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His rapport, distress and how much he discloses change with what you say. What he tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 50 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation and document.

source.cite: Common outpatient practice: a 50-minute session (the 'therapy hour')
source.note: Author's scenario timing; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

checkIn.label: Open-ended check-in: 'How has this week been?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give the client room to answer.

effects.finding: "Same as always. I like coming here. It helps to vent."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Daniel nods. "Yeah. It's the one hour I'm not pretending."

showData.label: Show him his GAD-7 scores across the eight weeks and look at them together

effects.log: You turn the chart toward him and look at the eight weeks together.

effects.finding: He studies it. "Huh. It's basically a flat line. Fifteen, sixteen, fifteen."

effects.log: Eight scores between 14 and 16: no meaningful change, still in the moderate-to-severe range.

askView.label: Ask what he makes of it, and what has and has not changed for him
askView.available: not talking and (dataReviewed and not hisView)

effects.log: You ask for his read on the chart and on his weeks.

effects.finding: "Talking helps in the moment. But the worry's the same. I still can't open emails from my boss."

explore.label: Explore what keeps the worry going: what he avoids, checks, or asks others to reassure him about

effects.log: You explore the patterns around his worry.

effects.finding: "I leave the boss's emails until night. I check my bank balance maybe ten times a day. And I ask Jess if things will be okay, a lot. She's tired of it."

options.label: Lay out the options with him: a structured cognitive-behavioral approach to worry, applied relaxation, or a medication evaluation, with what each involves
options.available: not talking and (dataReviewed and not optionsDiscussed)
options.why: Look at the data with him first.

effects.log: You explain the options in plain terms, what each would ask of him, and that the choice is his.

effects.finding: "I don't want pills yet. The cognitive one, with homework? I'd try that."

effects.log: When a client has not improved, a high-intensity psychological option or medication, chosen by his preference after information (NICE CG113).

chooseCbt.label: Agree on the switch together: weekly CBT for worry, starting with the avoidance and the checking

effects.log: You agree on the new approach together.

effects.finding: "Okay. Emails first. That's the one that's killing me."

goals.label: Rewrite the goals with him in measurable terms: GAD-7 under 10, the boss's emails opened within an hour, bank checks down to twice a day
goals.available: not talking and (maintainersExplored and not goalsRevised)
goals.why: Explore what keeps the worry going first.

effects.log: You turn 'reduce worry' into goals he can see and count.

effects.finding: He writes them in his phone. "Two bank checks. That's going to be hard. Good."

remeasureA.label: Keep the GAD-7 every session and set a review date six weeks out

effects.log: You agree to keep measuring and to review in six weeks.

effects.finding: "So we'll know if this one works."

continueSame.label: Tell him the dips to 14 are progress and continue as you have been

effects.log: You tell him the small dips show progress.
A point or two either way over eight weeks is noise, not progress; continuing unchanged ignores the data.

terminate.label: Tell him counseling does not seem to be working for him and suggest ending

effects.log: You suggest that counseling may not be for him.
Termination is for when a client no longer needs or is not benefiting from any counseling you could offer (ACA A.11.c). Here the plan, not Daniel, needs to change.

blame.label: Suggest the lack of progress is because he is not trying hard enough between sessions

effects.log: You suggest he is not putting in enough effort.

effects.finding: "You never gave me anything to do between sessions."

switchAlone.label: Tell him that, starting today, you are switching to CBT

effects.log: You announce the new approach.
Counseling plans are made jointly (ACA A.1.c); a change of approach needs his understanding and agreement.
You close the session.

read.title: Predict (not scored)
read.context: Eight weekly GAD-7 scores between 14 and 16, after an intake score of 16. What do they tell you?

choices.label: No meaningful change: review it with him and revise the plan together

effects.log: Prediction: revise together.

choices.feedback: Right. The scores sit in the moderate-to-severe range with no trend. Plans are reviewed and revised jointly when they are not working (ACA A.1.c), and he has a right to know and understand his results (ACA E.1.b).

choices.label: The dips to 14 show progress; keep going

effects.log: Prediction: progress.

choices.feedback: A point or two up and down over eight weeks is measurement noise. Continuing unchanged spends more of his time on an approach the data says is not working.

choices.label: He is not benefiting; end counseling

effects.log: Prediction: end it.

choices.feedback: The plan is not working; that is not the same as counseling not working for him. Change the plan before you consider ending.

formulation.question: Write your progress review: what the scores show, what keeps his worry going, and how and why the plan changed.

parts.label: What the data show
parts.criteria: GAD-7 14-16 for eight weeks after 16 at intake: no meaningful change, still moderate to severe; dips are noise; shared with him; his view matches (feels better in session, worry unchanged).
parts.modelAnswer: His GAD-7 has stayed between 14 and 16 for eight weeks after 16 at intake: no meaningful change, still in the moderate-to-severe range. I showed him the chart; he sees the same thing: talking helps in the hour, but the worry and the avoidance have not changed.

parts.label: The revised plan
parts.criteria: Maintainers named (avoidance, checking, reassurance seeking); options explained and chosen by his preference (CBT for worry; medication offered); measurable goals; GAD-7 each session and a review date; a joint decision (ACA A.1.c); no termination or blame.
parts.modelAnswer: His worry is kept going by avoiding his boss's emails, checking his bank balance about ten times a day and seeking reassurance. I explained the options; he chose a structured cognitive-behavioral approach over a medication evaluation for now. We rewrote the goals in measurable terms (GAD-7 under 10, emails within an hour, two bank checks a day) and will keep measuring each session, with a review in six weeks.

source.note: Rapport at the close of the session.

noProgress.rationale: Eight weeks of flat scores and no revision means more weeks of an approach that is not helping him.

revised.headline: Good: data used, with him, to change course
revised.body: You looked at the scores with him, named what maintains his worry, let him choose among real options, and made the goals measurable.

gaps.headline: Revised, with gaps

walkout.headline: He left
walkout.body: Flat scores are information about the plan, not a verdict on the client. Blame or an ending offer lands as failure.

stalled.headline: More of the same
stalled.body: Outcome measures are only useful if you act on them. Eight flat weeks call for a joint review and a different approach (ACA A.1.c).

dropped.headline: Ended instead of changed
dropped.body: Termination fits when a client no longer needs or cannot benefit from counseling (ACA A.11.c). Daniel has not had an evidence-based approach for worry yet.

time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Eight GAD-7 scores between 14 and 16 after 16 at intake mean no meaningful change: he is still in the moderate-to-severe range, and dips of a point or two are noise. Show him the chart and ask his view (ACA E.1.b), then explore what keeps the worry going: avoiding his boss's emails, checking his bank balance and seeking reassurance. Explain the options; after information, the choice between a structured cognitive-behavioral approach, applied relaxation and medication follows his preference (NICE CG113). He chooses CBT for worry. Rewrite the goals in measurable terms, keep measuring every session with a review date, and record the review. Do not call the noise progress, end counseling, blame him, or switch approaches without him (ACA A.1.c).
